Adult Common pike conger (Muraenesox bagio) are among the largest anguilliform predators in the Indo-West Pacific, with the maximum recorded total length reaching 200 cm [Li = 200 cm]. Specimens of this size, typically weighing around 9,000 grams [Wwi = around 9,000 grams], occupy the apex of the demersal fish assemblage on the continental shelf. Growth proceeds rapidly during the early benthic juvenile phase, and the transition to sexual maturity appears to be more strongly tied to size than to chronological age. Field surveys indicate that puberty is attained at a total length of 93.2 cm [Lp = 93.2 cm], a threshold that corresponds to a wet weight of approximately 980 grams [Wwp = approximately 980 grams]. The timing of these developmental milestones is ecologically significant because individuals below this size are rarely found in the spawning aggregations that form on the outer slope of the shelf break. Comparative data from other Muraenesocidae suggest that the size at maturity has been evolutionarily tuned to balance the high mortality rates experienced by smaller individuals against the energetic demands of egg production in a large-bodied predator.

Reproductive output in the Common pike conger is remarkably high, with females producing an estimated 195,120 oocytes per spawning event [N_R_i = 195,120 oocytes per spawning event] at a water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This per-event fecundity is accompanied by a spawning frequency of one event per year [F_R_i = one event per year], yielding an annual reproductive output exceeding 195,000 fertilized oocytes. The high fecundity per spawning represents one of the highest per-event reproductive outputs recorded among benthic marine teleosts and appears to be an adaptation to the high larval mortality typical of the pelagic egg phase in tropical waters. Egg diameters measured in captive spawnings range from 1.7 to 2.2 mm, consistent with values reported for the congener Congresox talabonoides, and the resulting wet weight of a newly hatched yolk-sac larva is estimated at 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams]. The combination of small initial size and high fecundity places this species firmly within the classic r-selected reproductive strategy observed in many large-bodied, long-lived marine fishes.

Embryonic development proceeds rapidly under the warm conditions typical of the species' tropical range. At a stable incubation temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the yolk-sac larvae emerge from the chorion after just 11 days [ab = 11 days], a short embryonic period that minimizes the vulnerability of the pelagic egg to predation. Upon hatching, the prolarvae measure only a few millimeters and rely entirely on their endogenous yolk reserves until mouth opening and the onset of exogenous feeding. The larval phase itself is characterized by a protracted planktonic duration, during which the juveniles undergo significant morphological transformation before settling to the benthos. The abbreviated embryogenesis at this temperature stands in contrast to the much longer incubation times observed in temperate anguilliform species, highlighting the pronounced effect of thermal regime on early life history in this lineage. This rapid development is a common feature among tropical eels adapted to warm, stable thermal environments.

The maximum lifespan of the Common pike conger is estimated at 38 years [am = 38 years] under the thermal conditions prevailing in its natural habitat, which typically average 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This longevity is inferred from growth increment analyses of otoliths collected from large adults and is consistent with the slow, asymptotic growth trajectory characteristic of the species after sexual maturation. Annual growth rings show that individuals invest heavily in somatic growth during the first decade of life, after which length increments diminish considerably as energy is increasingly diverted toward gamete production. Field recapture data from tagged specimens in the South China Sea corroborate this extended lifespan, with several individuals being recaptured more than two decades after initial marking. The persistence of individuals for nearly four decades (38 years) [am = 38 years] allows multiple spawning opportunities, enhancing the species' capacity to buffer against year-class failures in an unpredictable pelagic environment at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C].

Comparisons with other large-bodied marine eels reveal that the Common pike conger occupies an intermediate position on the life-history continuum between fast-growing, short-lived species and extreme longevity specialists. The asymptotic body mass of approximately 9,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 9,000 grams], coupled with the mass at puberty of 980 grams [Wwp = 980 grams], indicates that individuals more than double their somatic mass after reaching sexual maturity, a pattern consistent with indeterminate growth. This post-maturity growth allows older, larger females to produce disproportionately more eggs, a phenomenon that has been documented through the positive relationship between female length and fecundity in this species. The estimated maximum lifespan of 38 years [am = 38 years] at the prevailing habitat temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C] is substantially shorter than the century-scale lifespans reported for deep-sea eels but considerably longer than those of small-bodied tropical congrids. This intermediate longevity, combined with a high annual fecundity of 195,120 oocytes [Ri = annual fecundity of 195,120 oocytes] and a single spawning event per year [F_R_i = single spawning event per year], underscores the species' capacity for population resilience despite intensive fishing pressure across much of its range.
